source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat college students on text matrices, letter strings and verbal analogies. It was clearly worse on story analogies (Gentner et al. 1993 materials).
numbers: Story analogies: humans N=54; GPT-3 above chance in near analogy (binomial p=0.0039) but not far analogy (p=0.065); human vs GPT-3 OR=0.37, p=0.0003; 15 of 54 humans picked the analogous story on every trial. Other tasks: matrices N=40, letter strings N=57, verbal N=57.
limits: Zero-shot, text only. Possible training-data overlap on standard sets. Lewis and Mitchell show the letter-string result does not generalise.
agent_relevance: Far, surface-poor story mapping is the weak spot of an unaided model. That is where an explicit mapping step (O7) is meant to help.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) supplement: GPT-4 on story analogies
finding: A first GPT-4 test on the same story analogies: near-perfect on near analogies, some sensitivity to higher-order relations on far ones.
numbers: GPT-4 far analogy: two-sided binomial p=0.0039 against chance 0.5 (GPT-3 was p=0.065). Humans N=54.
limits: Small preliminary test, not a full replication. Authors expect scaling to help.
agent_relevance: Far-mapping ability rises with model size, so any scaffold gain must be re-measured on the model actually used.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Replicated Webb's letter-string task, then added counterfactual versions (permuted alphabets, symbol strings). Humans stayed high; GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 dropped sharply.
numbers: Humans (136 participants): 75.3% mean over counterfactual sets. Zero-shot GPT-3 48.8%, GPT-3.5 35.0%, GPT-4 45.2%. Original-task replication similar to Webb with some per-type differences.
limits: Letter-string domain only. Models passed a check that they understood the permuted alphabet, so the failure is in applying the rule, not in reading the alphabet.
agent_relevance: Rule transfer by similarity to training data fails under unfamiliar content. A typed relation list plus a code-checked mapping would not depend on that.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) error types and model generations
finding: Authors say GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are no better than GPT-3 on these problems, and GPT-3.5 is worse. They suggest the Webb result may come from similar sequences in training data.
numbers: Alternative-rule errors: humans 38.59%, GPT-4 22%, GPT-3 5.81%. Incorrect-rule errors over 30% for GPT-3 and GPT-4 vs about 15% for humans.
limits: The chat-tuning explanation is a conjecture in the paper.
agent_relevance: Newer chat models are not automatically better at mapping. Do not assume the base model maps well.

source: Hodel and West (2023) prompt-format dependence of letter-string analogies (seen as a citation in Lewis and Mitchell)
finding: Cited in Lewis and Mitchell: results on Webb's letter strings depend on prompt format; Lewis and Mitchell used the Hodel and West prompt for their GPT runs.
numbers: No numbers read first-hand.
limits: Seen only as a citation inside an opened paper.
agent_relevance: Any claim that a prompt helps mapping needs a fixed prompt format across arms.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogy corpus
finding: 24K story pairs annotated for entity similarity and relational similarity. LLMs pick analogies far worse than humans and favour surface-similar hard negatives.
numbers: Multiple choice: human 85.7%, random 25%, ChatGPT about 30%, text-davinci-003 37.1%, an SME-style structure method (Sultan and Shahaf) 44.9%. Models pick the analogy over hard negatives under 20% of the time where chance is 50%. Fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl matched zero-shot ChatGPT on generation.
limits: Distractors built to be hard. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Surface lure is the main failure. A mapper that scores relation overlap and ignores entity identity targets it directly.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Proverb-based benchmark in four conditions (far or near analogy against far or near distractor). LLMs are near human on near analogies and below chance on far analogies.
numbers: Humans: near analogies 97.9%, far 94.1%, average 96.0%. Models zero-shot: near analogies avg 75.0%, far analogies avg 39.6% (chance 50%). Partitions, model avg: near vs far distractor 76.9%, near-near 73.2%, far-far 45.3%, far analogy vs near distractor 33.9%. GPT-4 near human on near, below chance on far.
limits: Binary choice. Heuristics such as picking the dissimilar story can win the far-vs-near partition, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: The worst case (far analogy against near distractor, 33.9%) is the one O7 must handle; score relations, not topic overlap.

source: Sourati et al. (2023) ARN: guided prompting
finding: Prompts asking the model to use system mappings did not rescue the hardest partition in zero-shot.
numbers: Far analogy vs near distractor stayed at 33.9% average even with instructions asking for system mappings. A fine-tuned UnifiedQA-11B did on par or better than GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 on that partition (per the paper).
limits: Few-shot tables not fully extracted.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to ignore surface similarity does not work alone. A separate structural step is a better bet than a stronger instruction.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN: enhancing structural mapping with LLM-derived abstractions for narratives
finding: Closest published test of an SME-style loop with an LLM. The LLM splits stories into event units and abstracts them; a greedy one-to-one mapper (FAME-like) scores the match. Mapping raw event phrases is poor; with abstraction it is competitive.
numbers: Qwen3-8B, StoryAnalogy-MCQ (4 choices, chance 25%): mapping on raw events 0.17; best abstraction 0.46 vs best LLM-only 0.41 (CoT). Llama-3.1-8B: 0.45 vs 0.28 LLM-only. ARN far analogy: Qwen mapper 0.47 vs zero-shot 0.52; Llama mapper 0.46 vs 0.42. ARN near analogy: LLM better (Qwen CoT 0.79 vs mapper 0.69; Llama 0.76 vs 0.73).
limits: 8B models only. Score uses cosine similarity of text embeddings, not full SME. Hardest far-near cases stay below 50% in every setting. Preprint.
agent_relevance: LLM extract plus code map helps on far analogies and hurts on near ones. Use the mapper when surface cues are poor, not by default.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN ablations: abstraction level
finding: The best abstraction depends on the data. Evaluative labels helped on short MCQ stories but slightly hurt on ARN. Stage abstraction hurt on short stories.
numbers: Qwen MCQ: conceptual only 0.41, conceptual plus evaluative 0.46. ARN near (Qwen): 0.67 without evaluative vs 0.63 with. Llama MCQ: stage abstraction 0.24 and 0.27 vs 0.45 conceptual. Beam output: top-3 mappings for ARN, top-2 for MCQ.
limits: Dataset-specific; number of runs per setting not stated.
agent_relevance: The typed relation list must be chosen per task. Do not fix one abstraction level in the schema.

source: Jacob, Shani, Shahaf (2023) FAME: Flexible, scalable analogy mappings engine (EMNLP)
finding: Needs only entity names. Gets relations from ConceptNet, Open IE, Quasimodo and GPT-3.5, then runs a beam search for the best mapping with a relaxed one-to-one rule.
numbers: 2x2 near 85%, far 77.5% (80 problems from Green et al. 2010; chance 33.3%). Extended problems (36, average domain size 3.3): 77.8% perfect, chance 13.1%; right answer in top-2 83.3%, top-3 91.7%. Versus LRME on 19 noun-only problems: 84.2% vs 75%.
limits: Small human-built sets. Could not compare with SME directly because of its input needs; used published LRME figures instead.
agent_relevance: LLM-generated relations can feed a mapper. Top-3 candidates are far better than top-1, so keep several mappings (SME also returns up to three).

source: Jacob et al. (2023) FAME ablation and GPT-3.5 baseline
finding: Plain GPT-3.5 looked as good as the mapper on classical 2x2 problems that are on the web, but fell on larger unseen mapping problems.
numbers: GPT-3.5 with ':' prompt: near 92%, far 80%, extended 44%. With '->' prompt: 88%, 80%, 58%. FAME: 85.0%, 77.5%, 77.8%. Ablation: GPT-3 as only knowledge source 57.5% near, 50% far, 66.7% extended; dropping Open IE gave 58.3% extended.
limits: Authors found some answers by simple web search, so leakage is likely on 2x2 sets. text-davinci-002 era.
agent_relevance: Large mapping problems (many entities) are where a code mapper beats a bare model. Toy problems hide the gap.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, J. Memory and Language 145
finding: Mapping words to letter or symbol strings. The best models (GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-405B) match humans in many conditions but react differently to semantic distractors and numeric structure.
numbers: Match-to-reference about 0.8 (Claude 3 and humans) and 0.9 (GPT-4) in one condition, about 0.5 for Llama-405B. Random-final-word distractor lowered Claude 3 by about 0.5 and GPT-4 by about 0.8. In another task humans and Claude 3 about 0.7, GPT-4 and Llama-405B about 0.35. Chain-of-thought tried only on Claude 3.
limits: Match to reference, not accuracy. Closed models with unknown training data. Human sample sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Behaviour is fragile to irrelevant semantic content. Strip content into typed roles before mapping.

source: Inani, Kabra, Marupudi, Varma (2025) Modeling understanding of story-based analogies using LLMs
finding: Re-tests the Gentner 1993 / Webb story set (18 problems). A self-generated-hint prompt raised accuracy. Models beat humans overall, but items hard for humans are not hard for models.
numbers: Humans 0.847, GPT-3 0.75 (Webb). BERT embedding cosine picks the true analogy on 78% of items; item-level correlation with human difficulty r=-0.032 (p=0.899). Conventional prompt: gpt-4o-mini 0.7011, gpt-4o 0.8233, Llama-3.1-8B 0.6528, Llama-3.1-70B 0.8538. Enhanced (hint) prompt higher in both families, best value 0.9150 (table layout garbled in extraction, cell-to-model mapping uncertain). Larger models about 15 points better.
limits: Only 18 problems. One enhanced-prompt setting had human-model item correlation r=0.526 (p=0.025); which setting is unclear in extracted text.
agent_relevance: A cheap explain-the-relational-match-first hint helps. Still worth testing whether code scoring adds beyond it.

source: Inani et al. (2025) citing earlier work: answer-order and paraphrase effects
finding: Reports that GPT-4 story-analogy accuracy depends on answer position and on paraphrase, while humans are less affected.
numbers: GPT-4 89% when the correct answer is first vs 61% when second (as reported). Paraphrased stories: GPT-4 86% to 72%, humans 78% to 70%.
limits: Second-hand: attributed to Lewis and Mitchell, but I did not find these figures in the Lewis and Mitchell paper I opened (2402.08955); the source may be another paper.
agent_relevance: Randomise candidate order and run paraphrases when scoring analogue choice.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The curious case of analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Interpretability study. Relational information sits in mid-to-upper layers in correct cases and is missing in wrong cases, but applying it to new entities is a second bottleneck. Structural alignment between story pairs is stronger when the model succeeds.
numbers: Patching hidden states repairs up to 38.4% of failed cases (Gemma-7B); gains of +32.3% (Llama-2-13B) and +35.6% (Qwen2.5-14B) reported in the same table. Linear probe separating analogical from lexically similar stories averages 82.9% on layers 20 to 30.
limits: Open-weight 7B to 14B models; StoryAnalogy and proportional analogies. Alignment link is correlational.
agent_relevance: Failures are as often in applying a relation as in finding it. A candidate-inference step with an explicit check addresses the application half.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Prompt makes the model write relevant example problems before solving. Analogy used as an agent prompt, with no explicit mapping or score.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, few-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated exemplars 77.8. MATH: 33.0, 33.9, 34.9, 37.3. Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-3.5: 8, 9, 11, 13, 15 (knowledge plus exemplars). GPT-4 Acc@1: 16, 16, 17, 17, 19.
limits: Gains of 1 to 4 points on standard sets; no variance in the text read. Row-to-method order inferred from garbled table text.
agent_relevance: Small gain from self-generated analogues. Supports analogy at impasses only (SCHEMA O7), not on routine items.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024) Thought propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Agent loop that proposes and solves analogous problems, then reuses their solutions to fix the first answer. Also used in a plan loop for ALFWorld.
numbers: Shortest-path optimal rate, 0-shot: GPT-3.5 TP 0.65 vs IO 0.33, CoT 0.26, ToT 0.22; GPT-4 TP 0.88 vs IO 0.78; PaLM-2 TP 0.36 vs CoT 0.24. Abstract: +12% shortest path, +13% creative-writing preference, +15% ALFWorld completion (134 tasks). 100 shortest-path and 100 writing problems.
limits: No explicit structure mapping; the analogues are neighbour problems in a graph. Higher token cost; a second layer gave marginal gain.
agent_relevance: An analogy-in-agent-loop result with measured gain, but its analogues are structurally trivial, so it says little about O7 on distant analogues.

source: Turney (2008) The Latent Relation Mapping Engine: algorithm and experiments (JAIR)
finding: Removes SME's hand-coded input by using corpus statistics for word-pair relations, then searches mappings by relational similarity. Reaches human level on 20 mapping problems.
numbers: 20 problems (10 science analogies, 10 metaphors); humans N=22: LRME 91.5% vs human average 87.6% (not significantly different); best attribute-similarity method 76.8%. LRA on SAT 374 questions 56% vs human 57%.
limits: Needed a large corpus and an exhaustive search; small problem set; average m=7 so m! is manageable.
agent_relevance: An earlier non-LLM way to build the typed input. An LLM extracting relations now does this job (FAME, YARN).

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett, Gentner (2017) Extending SME to create and use large-scale models, Cognitive Science 41
finding: Describes greedy merge, incremental mapping, structural evaluation of candidate inferences, ubiquitous predicates and match filters. Greedy merge keeps SME polynomial.
numbers: Complexity O(n^2 log n). Greedy merge gave the same best mapping as exhaustive merge in 52 of 56 analogies (93%); 4 failures. Up to 3 interpretations returned by default. Run time correlated well with n^2 log n.
limits: The 56-analogy test (Forbus and Oblinger 1990) used hand-built representations. Greedy fails when many large kernels conflict.
agent_relevance: A small code mapper is cheap enough to run on every analogue candidate. Return several mappings, not one.

source: Gentner and Forbus (2025) The structure-mapping engine: a multidecade interaction between psychology and AI, Current Directions in Psychological Science
finding: Review. SME works over representations from language, vision or reasoning systems. LLMs have been used with a symbolic language system; whether generative AI can do analogical processing without a symbol system is called an open question.
numbers: CogSketch at the 61st percentile on Raven's (Lovett and Forbus 2017). Complexity O(n^2 log n). SME in use for 4 decades.
limits: Review by the theory's authors, not an independent test. The Raven's figure conflicts with the higher one in c23.
agent_relevance: The authors call LLM-without-symbols an open question, which supports testing a hybrid.

source: Falkenhainer, Forbus, Gentner (1989) The structure-mapping engine: algorithm and examples (Artificial Intelligence 41)
finding: Original SME paper, cited by several opened papers. The Rutherford atom example is reported through a 2026 survey: three interpretations ranked by structural evaluation score.
numbers: Best interpretation SES=6.03 (nucleus to sun, electron to planet); worst SES=1.87 (equates sun mass with electron mass), as reported in the 2026 survey.
limits: Numbers seen second-hand through the survey; I did not read the original text for this line.
agent_relevance: A reference toy case for testing any new mapper and its score.

source: Minimal Cognitive Grid ranking of SME, CogSketch, METCL and GPT-3.5/4/4o (2026)
finding: Survey says there is no strong evidence that LLMs satisfy systematicity, and that LLMs lack explicit inferential projection. It reports SME and CogSketch results on human tests.
numbers: Quoted from Lovett et al.: SME/CogSketch on Raven's sections B to E 44/48 (converted 55/60, 91.66%); the 4 misses were among the 6 hardest for humans. Evans geometric analogies: all 20 matched the human-preferred answer (human N=34); reaction-time correlation r=0.59 normal mode, r=0.75 shape-identicality mode.
limits: Secondary survey; figures from Lovett papers I did not open. Conflicts with 61st percentile in c21.
agent_relevance: Gives a human-error-matching benchmark for the mapper and states the LLM gap on systematicity.

source: Stevenson et al. (2023) via 2026 survey: LLM proportional-analogy success driven by association
finding: As quoted in the survey: LLMs reach about the accuracy of children aged 7 to 12 on A:B::C:? analogies, driven by association between C and D rather than relation structure.
numbers: No numbers read first-hand.
limits: Second-hand, from the survey.
agent_relevance: A reason not to trust accuracy alone; check that the model's answer uses relations.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) SCAR via 2026 survey: scientific analogies with confusable distractors
finding: As quoted in the survey: SCAR has over 400 science analogies with semantically confusable distractors; GPT-4 often picks structurally wrong completions.
numbers: Count of problems only (over 400).
limits: Second-hand; no accuracy values read.
agent_relevance: Candidate benchmark for scoring a scaffold on science-style transfer.

source: Wachowiak and Gromann (2023) via 2026 survey: GPT-3 source-domain inference for metaphor
finding: As quoted in the survey: GPT-3 infers an appropriate metaphorical source domain from a target at 65% accuracy.
numbers: 65% (second-hand).
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Choosing a source domain (the retrieval half) is done passably by models.

source: Nakos and Forbus (2023) Using large language models in the Companion cognitive architecture
finding: Cited in Gentner and Forbus 2025: an LLM used with a symbolic language system inside Companion to improve learning by reading.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Paper not opened; only the citation seen.
agent_relevance: An existing example of an LLM feeding SME-style structured input in a running architecture.

source: Gentner and Forbus (2025) on hybrids: vector embeddings inside SME structural evaluation (Liang et al. 2016)
finding: Some SME versions use distributed representations as one input to structural scoring. SME remains a symbolic model.
numbers: No accuracy given in the review.
limits: Details only in the cited paper.
agent_relevance: Supports a design where an LLM or embedding supplies relation similarity and code applies one-to-one and systematicity rules.

source: Search coverage note for this run
finding: No head-to-head test of a full SME run against LLMs on the same items was found in the sources read. The closest are YARN (greedy mapper with embedding score) and FAME (beam mapper).
numbers: n/a
limits: Web search and the arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs ran out of quota after about 12 searches, so this may be a search gap.
agent_relevance: Treat the claim that no explicit SME-in-LLM-loop study exists as unconfirmed.
